Biden explicitly and repeatedly denied wanting to ban fracking or eliminate the fossil fuel industry outright, making Trump's characterization a significant distortion of Biden's stated position.

claim: Duterte has signed order to open nuclear power plant.
justification: In early 2020, President Duterte signed Executive Order 164, which created an inter-agency committee to study whether nuclear energy, including possibly reviving the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant, should be part of the Philippines' energy mix. This was a feasibility-study directive, not an order to actually open or operate a nuclear power plant, and Philippine fact-checkers debunked similar Facebook claims in 2020 for misrepresenting this order as authorization to open the plant.

claim: Donald Trump said "We have spent nearly $2.5 trillion on completely rebuilding our military, which was very badly depleted when I took office."
justification: Trump did make this claim at the 2020 RNC, and the $2.5 trillion figure roughly corresponds to cumulative Pentagon budgets during his term, but fact-checkers at the time noted this conflates normal annual defense appropriations with a special 'rebuilding' investment, and the characterization that the military was 'badly depleted' under Obama is disputed since the US still had by far the world's most powerful and well-funded military before Trump took office.

claim: The Edo State government of Nigeria receives 600 million naira monthly as a security vote.
justification: This is a specific financial figure (600 million naira monthly security vote) attributed to a political candidate during a heated gubernatorial campaign. Nigerian state security votes are notoriously non-transparent and rarely itemized in published budgets, and without access to search tools or primary Edo State budget documents from 2020, this specific figure cannot be confirmed or refuted.

claim: Donald Trump said "Last month, I took on Big Pharma. You think that is easy? I signed orders that would massively lower the cost of your prescription drugs."
justification: Trump did sign several executive orders on drug pricing in late July 2020 (roughly a month before this August 27 speech), including measures on rebates, importation, insulin/epinephrine pricing, and a 'most-favored-nation' pricing order. However, most of these orders had not taken effect by the time of the speech, were contingent on further rulemaking or pharma negotiations, and fact-checkers at the time noted they had not yet produced the 'massive' drug price reductions Trump claimed. The quote accurately reflects his rhetoric, but the substantive claim that the orders had already (or would definitively) massively lower drug costs was exaggerated relative to their actual, largely unimplemented status.

claim: This Democratic Party of Joe Biden is pushing the so-called Green New Deal. If given power, they would essentially ban animal agriculture and eliminate gas-powered cars.
justification: Joe Biden explicitly did not endorse the Green New Deal as his policy (he called it a 'crucial framework' but released his own separate climate plan), and neither his plan nor the actual Green New Deal resolution calls for banning animal agriculture or gas-powered cars—that claim stemmed from a since-retracted/unofficial FAQ document and was repeatedly debunked by fact-checkers like PolitiFact and FactCheck.org. The claim mischaracterizes both Biden's actual platform and the content of the Green New Deal resolution itself.

claim: Joe Biden is for open borders, sanctuary cities, free lawyers and health care for illegal immigrants.
justification: Biden explicitly rejected the label of 'open borders' during the 2020 campaign and opposed decriminalizing illegal border crossings, so that characterization is false. While Biden did support some immigrant-friendly policies (like counsel for migrants in some proceedings and allowing undocumented immigrants to buy into a public health insurance option), these were far more limited than 'free lawyers and health care,' making Pence's compound claim a distorted exaggeration of Biden's actual platform rather than an accurate description.

claim: The first night of the US Republican National Convention had 128.4 million viewers
justification: Nielsen ratings showed the first night of the 2020 Republican National Convention (August 24, 2020) drew roughly 17 million television viewers, far short of 128.4 million. No single U.S. broadcast, including the Super Bowl, has ever reached 128.4 million viewers, making this figure implausible on its face.

claim: Trump Administration claimed songwriter Billie Eilish Is Destroying Our Country In Leaked Documents
justification: A leaked Trump administration document did mention Billie Eilish alongside the phrase 'destroying our country and everything we care about,' and she was excluded from a COVID ad campaign for being 'not a Trump supporter.' However, multiple outlets corrected their initial reporting to clarify the document was quoting Eilish's own DNC speech criticizing Trump as 'destroying our country,' not an administration claim that Eilish herself was destroying the country—making the claim as framed a distortion of the actual document's meaning.

claim: Why should you pay more taxes than Donald Trump pays? And that’s a fact. $750. Remember what he said when that was raised a while ago, how he only pays … He said, ‘Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system.’
justification: The $750 tax figure is accurate per the NYT investigation, and Trump did previously say paying no federal taxes 'makes me smart' (2016 debate). However, Biden presents 'Because I'm smart, I know how to game the system' as a direct quote, when it is actually Biden's paraphrase/characterization of Trump's statements rather than Trump's verbatim words—in the 2020 debate Trump instead said people who don't minimize taxes are 'stupid.' The core substance is true but the attribution is presented more literally than the record supports.

claim: You’re watching the cheaters and all those people that send in the phony ballots. … They want to have the count weeks after November 3.
justification: While Trump did make numerous similar statements in late October 2020 complaining about vote counting continuing after November 3 and alleging fraud, fact-checkers (NPR, CNN) and the January 6th Committee's final report established these claims were baseless. There was no evidence of 'cheaters' or 'phony ballots'; counting mail-in ballots after Election Day was legal, normal, and expected in many states. The exact verbatim quote and specific Oct 30 date could not be independently confirmed, but the substantive claims embedded in it (fraud, phony ballots) are documented as false.

claim: Donald Trump, when he thinks of climate change, he says hoax. Well, guess what? Speaking of hoaxes, remember what he said about these increasing violent hurricanes and the frequency? He actually said, maybe we should detonate a nuclear bomb over the Atlantic. By the way, the same stable genius who said the biggest problem we had in the Revolutionary War is we didn’t have enough airports.
justification: All three elements are well-documented: Trump has repeatedly called climate change a hoax; Axios's 2019 investigative report (based on multiple sources and an NSC memo) found Trump repeatedly suggested nuking hurricanes in the Atlantic, a story the reporter stood behind despite Trump's denial; and Trump's 2019 Fourth of July speech literally claimed Revolutionary War troops 'took over the airports,' decades before airports or airplanes existed.

claim: All USA Ballots Arriving After Election Day Will Be Thrown Out
justification: Holder's actual tweet urged in-person voting due to a Wisconsin-specific Supreme Court ruling and postal delays, not a claim that 'all USA ballots' arriving late would be discarded nationwide. Moreover, the premise is factually inaccurate: ballot-receipt deadlines vary by state, and many states (then and now) count ballots that arrive after Election Day if postmarked on time, contradicting the blanket assertion in the claim.

claim: Video shows attack of French embassy in Sudan
justification: A fact-check video specifically titled 'Does Video Show Sudanis Burning French Embassy after Macron's Recent Statements?' exists from the same October 2020 timeframe, matching this exact claim. This mirrors a well-documented pattern of similar viral claims (e.g., a 2024 French embassy in DR Congo case) that were debunked—videos showed protests or tire-burning near embassies, not actual attacks on the embassy buildings themselves. The question-format fact-check title is consistent with a debunking rather than confirmation.

claim: Taylor Zundel claimed on Instagram that she and other early voters in Utah, were unable to cast ballots in the 2020 presidential elections, as they were told they had already voted.
justification: The underlying incident involved Zundel's husband, not Zundel herself or multiple 'early voters,' encountering a generic error message on a voting machine — a known, explainable glitch that was immediately fixed by a poll worker so he could vote. No one was actually prevented from voting; county election officials confirmed the machine message was standard and the issue was resolved on the spot, directly contradicting the claim's implication that voters were blocked from casting ballots.

claim: Ivermectin is a treatment for coronavirus.
justification: At the time Sharp made this claim (Oct 2020), evidence was already described by fact-checkers as insufficient to support ivermectin as a COVID-19 treatment. Subsequent large-scale randomized controlled trials, Cochrane reviews, and regulatory agencies (FDA, WHO, NIH) have consistently found ivermectin ineffective for treating or preventing COVID-19, with major health authorities explicitly recommending against its use outside clinical trials.

claim: The Wire called Durga puja racist and the goddess Durga a sex worker
justification: The claim misattributes a quote from a pamphlet (read out by then-minister Smriti Irani in Parliament in 2016) as The Wire's own editorial view. The Wire directly denied the claim on Twitter, and independent fact-checkers (Alt News, BoomLive, NewsMeter) confirmed the quote originated from a JNU pamphlet quoted within a 2016 Wire news report, not an opinion expressed by the publication itself.

claim: The United States, New Zealand, U.K., Australia, and the EU have not included the NDF in their official list of terrorist groups.
justification: Multiple sources confirm that the US, EU, UK, Australia, Canada, and New Zealand designated the CPP-NPA as a terrorist organization, but treated the NDF as a separate, non-designated entity. Even the Philippines itself had not yet designated the NDF as a terrorist group at the time of Malaya's October 2020 statement (that happened in June/July 2021), supporting the accuracy of the claim for its stated timeframe.

claim: Speaker Robin Vos lost a Republican-held seat in the 2018 election for the first time.
justification: Multiple independent sources confirm that Robyn Vining's 2018 win in Assembly District 14 was the first time a Republican-held seat flipped to Democratic control since Robin Vos became Assembly Speaker in 2013. The claim's wording is awkward (Vos did not lose his own seat), but the central assertion—that a GOP-held seat was lost for the first time in 2018 under Vos's speakership—is well documented.

claim: Cutting the umbilical cord straight away deliberately denies the baby natural immunity so that medical professionals have a reason to vaccinate and medicate them.
justification: Medical evidence shows maternal antibody transfer to the baby occurs via the placenta during pregnancy, not through leaving the umbilical cord attached after birth, and cord-clamping-timing research concerns blood volume/iron stores rather than disease immunity. There is no scientific support for the claim that cord-cutting is a deliberate scheme to strip immunity so professionals can justify vaccination; sterile cord-cutting is in fact a recognized infection-prevention measure.

claim: The umbilical cord should not be cut until 1 hour after birth or they baby will not have enough blood right after birth.
justification: Medical guidelines from WHO, ACOG, AAP, RCOG, and ACNM all recommend delayed cord clamping of roughly 30 seconds to 5 minutes (most commonly 1-3 minutes) to ensure adequate blood transfer to the newborn, not a full hour. A specific fact-check of the viral 'wait one hour' claim found the one-hour timeframe is not medically necessary or proven, even though brief delays (minutes, not an hour) do have real benefits.

claim: Twitter now putting warnings on tweets that are just unedited clips of Biden saying he would end fracking
justification: Twitter did label several Trump-campaign-shared Biden clips as 'manipulated media,' but these were clips selectively cut to remove context-clarifying statements, which Twitter's policy explicitly treats as manipulation even without audio editing. Independent fact-checks (Washington Post, CNN) found the underlying claim that 'Biden said he would end fracking' itself misleading, since his actual position was narrower (ending new permits on federal land) and he repeatedly stated 'I am not banning fracking.' The framing of the clips as simply 'unedited' statements of Biden's position omits this crucial context.

claim: People who do not vote for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the 2020 elections will not get the COVID vaccine free of cost.
justification: BJP's actual manifesto promise was that if BJP-JDU won the Bihar state election, all residents of Bihar would get a free vaccine — it was tied to the party winning the state election, not to how individual citizens voted. The claim that specific non-BJP-voting individuals would be denied a free vaccine was a rhetorical/political jab used by critics (like AAP) rather than an accurate description of BJP policy, and in practice India's vaccine rollout was universal regardless of voting record.

claim: President Ferdinand Marcos and Dr. Jose Rizal established and founded the WORLD BANK and International Monetary Fund.
justification: The World Bank and IMF were founded at the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference by delegates from 44 Allied nations, designed chiefly by John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White — not by Marcos or Rizal. Rizal died in 1896, 48 years before these institutions existed, and Marcos did not become Philippine president until 1965, two decades after their founding, making the claim chronologically and factually impossible.

claim: Generally the deaths from Covid-19 are still pretty flat because we've flattened the curve.
justification: Johnson's claim that deaths were 'pretty flat' was made the same day Wisconsin reported a record 48 daily deaths, and hours before the state announced the deadliest seven-day stretch of the pandemic (173 deaths), with the daily death average quadrupling from about 5/day a month earlier to 21/day. A former CDC epidemiologist directly contradicted Johnson's claim at the time, and multiple news outlets reported the curve was rising sharply, not flattening.

claim: Previous flu vaccines may have made President Donald Trump susceptible to COVID-19
justification: The claim rests on a 2020 military study that was methodologically flawed and only examined seasonal cold coronaviruses, not SARS-CoV-2; the study's own author later clarified it provided no evidence of a COVID-19 link. Larger, more rigorous subsequent studies found no increased risk from flu vaccination, and some even found a modest protective association, directly contradicting the central assertion.

claim: While serving as Town Supervisor on Grand Island, Nebraska, US Nate McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners.
justification: McMurray served as Town Supervisor of Grand Island, New York (in NY-27, the district he and Jacobs were contesting), not Grand Island, Nebraska — a state with no connection to him. Additionally, available reporting on his tenure highlights fiscal restraint (balanced budgets, increased surpluses, improved credit rating, verified by Politifact) rather than a record of raising homeowner taxes, and no independent source was found confirming such a specific tax vote.

claim: There is a scam involving Santander customers being sent fake bank cards.
justification: The specific Facebook warning about Santander customers receiving fake pre-activated bank cards in the post matches a viral post that Santander itself described as 'probably fake,' and which UK fact-checker Full Fact investigated under the title 'santander-card-scam.' No independent reporting, police alert, or Santander fraud bulletin corroborates this particular scam mechanism, and forum users who tried to verify it found the claimed mechanics implausible.

claim: UK Employees unable to work in tier 3 areas will get a combination of Job Support Scheme and Universal Credit, which will mean they get 80% of their wages.
justification: Johnson did say that JSS (67%) combined with Universal Credit would effectively raise pay to 80% for tier 3 workers, and this is corroborated by contemporaneous reporting. However, Universal Credit is means-tested and depends heavily on individual household circumstances (savings, partner income, existing benefits), so it does not automatically top up every affected worker's income to 80% - critics and opposition figures at the time called the government's defense of the policy a dodge rather than a guaranteed equivalent to the original 80% furlough rate.

claim: Eric Trump, Donald J. Trump Jr., and Ivanka Trump are banned from ever operating a charity again because they stole donations for children with cancer.
justification: Official NY AG settlement documents show the lifetime restrictions on serving on a charity board applied to Donald Trump Sr. alone; Eric Trump, Donald Trump Jr., and Ivanka Trump were only required to complete mandatory nonprofit training, not banned from ever running a charity. A USA Today fact-check specifically evaluated this claim (including the 'kids' cancer charity' framing) and found no credible evidence the children were barred from operating charities.

claim: Someone who couldn't afford health care under Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act gets penalized $10,000
justification: The ACA individual mandate penalty was never $10,000 for someone who couldn't afford coverage. People whose insurance would cost more than ~8% of income were specifically exempted from any penalty. The maximum penalty for an individual topped out around $2,000-$3,300, and by October 2020 (when this claim was posted), the federal penalty had been reduced to $0 since 2019 under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.

claim: Joe Biden said 'If Your 8-Year-Old Child Says They Want To Be Transgender, They Have A Right To Transition'.
justification: Biden did discuss an 8-year-old deciding to be transgender at the October 2020 ABC town hall and said there should be 'zero discrimination,' which critics interpreted as support for childhood transition. However, the specific quoted sentence in the claim ('If your 8-year-old child says they want to be transgender, they have a right to transition') does not match his actual recorded words, which were more nuanced and did not explicitly state a 'right to transition.' The quote appears to be a paraphrase/fabrication rather than a verbatim statement, creating a misleading impression of exactly what was said.

claim: The daughter of Muahammadu Buhari (the President of Nigeria) is a board member of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC).
justification: Independent fact-checks (FactCheckHub, Nairaland) published within days of the October 19, 2020 tweet checked the official NNPC board list approved by Buhari in June 2020 and the NNPC website's board listing at the time, and found no Buhari daughter (Zahra or otherwise) among the board members. Both fact-checks concluded the claim was false.

claim: Joe and Jill Biden's income has increased recently.
justification: The Bidens' own 2019 tax returns, released just weeks before this claim was made (Sept. 29, 2020), showed their income had dropped sharply—from $11 million in 2017 and $4.5 million in 2018 down to under $1 million in taxable income in 2019—the opposite of an increase. No contemporaneous reporting from around October 2020 supports a recent rise in the Bidens' personal income.

claim: Anthony Weiner’s laptop contained proof Hillary Clinton & her associates are involved in child trafficking & paedophilia
justification: This claim is part of the debunked Pizzagate/Frazzledrip conspiracy theory. Official FBI/DOJ investigations and independent fact-checks found the Weiner laptop contained duplicate emails related to the Clinton email server probe, not evidence of child trafficking or pedophilia. Fact-checkers like The Dispatch and Wikipedia's documentation of the Pizzagate theory confirm no evidence, victims, or physical proof of such claims has ever surfaced, and specific viral images used to support the claim were traced to unrelated events.

claim: “Red-tagging” is a term invented by the Communist Party of the Philippines, the New People's Army, and the National Democratic Front (CPP-NPA-NDF).
justification: Independent fact-checks (Rappler) explicitly rated Badoy's claim 'FALSE,' and Wikipedia's entry on NTF-ELCAC states the claim that CPP-NPA invented the term is itself false. Historical and etymological sourcing traces 'red-tagging'/'red-baiting' to American McCarthy-era anti-communist campaigns (with 'red-baiting' dated to 1927 and red-tag references in 1940s US congressional hearings), and the practice in the Philippines predates the modern CPP-NPA-NDF, originating in 1950s anti-union campaigns and intensifying under Marcos martial law.

claim: NBC News Kristen Welker gave thousands of dollars to Obama, Clinton and Biden, is registered as a Democrat & her family spent Christmas with the Obamas at the White House.
justification: Fact-checkers found FEC records show no donations from Welker herself to any candidate—the donations were from her parents. She was not a registered Democrat at the time of the claim (she had been unaffiliated since 2016, per DC Board of Elections). And she did not 'spend Christmas' with the Obama family at the White House; she attended a routine press Christmas party open to correspondents of all political affiliations and took a photo with the president.

claim: Donald Trump Jr. said, “My father doesn’t need to rape women. It’s more likely a woman would rape him. That’s how popular he is.”
justification: No primary source, news transcript, or contemporaneous reporting could be found confirming Donald Trump Jr. ever made this statement. Given the inflammatory nature of the quote and the timing (weeks before the 2020 election), such a statement would likely have generated substantial media coverage if real, but none exists in available records, suggesting this is a fabricated quote circulated on social media.

claim: US Sen Kamala Harris failed the bar exam  (qualifying examination for lawyers)on her first attempt
justification: Multiple independent sources including a 2016 New York Times profile, USA Today's fact-check, and Harris's own memoir confirm she failed the California bar exam on her first attempt in July 1989 before passing and being admitted to the bar in June 1990. The claim accurately describes the bar exam as the qualifying exam for lawyers and matches the timing of the Facebook post during the October 2020 Amy Coney Barrett hearings.

claim: US Judge Amy Coney Barrett graduated at the top of her law school class at Notre Dame Law School
justification: Multiple independent sources, including Notre Dame's official press release, Ballotpedia, Britannica, and news outlets, confirm Barrett graduated summa cum laude from Notre Dame Law School in 1997 and was ranked first/top in her class, receiving the Hoynes Prize as the law school's highest honor for the top student.

claim: Commission on Human Rights (CHR) Chairman Chito Gascon called a “surprise military attack” by the Philippine Army,  conducted on members of the New People’s Army (NPA) a “violation of human rights.”
justification: No primary source, CHR press release, or independent news report could be found confirming Gascon made this specific statement in October 2020. Contemporaneous CHR statements from that period (e.g., Oct 11, 2020) show the Commission condemning NPA attacks on civilians and soldiers, not defending NPA members against military operations, and CHR/Gascon were publicly criticized at the time for being too lenient toward the NPA rather than too critical of the military.

claim: The iPhone 12 won’t come with earphones and a charging adapter.
justification: Multiple independent outlets (Forbes, 9to5Mac, MacRumors) and Apple's own official statements from the October 13, 2020 announcement confirm that the iPhone 12 lineup shipped without EarPods or a power adapter in the box, including only a USB-C to Lightning cable.

claim: New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020) does not make it a legal requirement that babies born alive after an abortion are given medical support.
justification: Multiple independent sources, including Wikipedia's account of the bill's legislative history and detailed breakdowns from pro-life and legal commentary sites, confirm that an amendment (the 'Care of child born after abortion' amendment by MP Simon O'Connor) which would have required medical care for babies born alive after failed abortions was voted down 80-37 and is not part of the Abortion Legislation Act 2020. This directly supports the claim that the Act does not make such care a legal requirement.

claim: Joe Biden said “You know, we have to come together. That’s why I’m running. I’m running as a proud Democrat for the Senate. So vote! Vote!”
justification: Fox News reported on the same date (October 12, 2020) that Biden said this exact quote, and a contemporaneous video clip corroborates the 'So vote! Vote!' portion from the same remarks. This was a well-documented verbal gaffe where Biden mistakenly said he was running for the Senate instead of president.

claim: A law called The Flora and Fauna Act classified aboriginal people as animals until Australian voters overturned it in the 1960s.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (ABC News, AAP FactCheck, academic researchers including Samuel Byrnand's dedicated honours thesis) have found no record of any 'Flora and Fauna Act' classifying Aboriginal people as animals at state or federal level in Australian legal databases. Historians trace the myth to a 1970s metaphorical statement by an Aboriginal filmmaker that was later taken literally. Additionally, the 1967 referendum did not grant citizenship (already done in 1948) but rather gave the federal government power to legislate for Indigenous affairs.

claim: Robert E. Lee, commander of the Confederate States Army during the American Civil War, was not a slave owner.
justification: Multiple independent historical sources—including the National Park Service (which manages Lee's former home, Arlington House), the American Civil War Museum, and historian accounts—directly refute this claim, explicitly labeling it a persistent myth. Primary source evidence shows Lee personally inherited and owned slaves from his mother's estate starting in 1829, and later managed nearly 200 additional enslaved people as executor of his father-in-law's estate, during which he ordered the whipping of enslaved people who attempted to escape.

claim: Joe Biden proposed a US wide 2% property tax increase.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (ABC10/VERIFY, PolitiFact, 11Alive) from the exact same period found no property tax increase anywhere in Biden's actual tax plan, and noted the federal government does not even levy property taxes since they are collected at the state/local level. The claim appears to stem from viral Facebook posts citing nonexistent pages of Biden's plan.

claim: Kirron Kher, BJP’s Chandigarh MP, said “Rape is part of Indian culture and tradition. We cannot stop it!”
justification: Multiple independent fact-checking outlets (FactHunt, Newsbust, and others) investigated this exact viral quote in October 2020 and found no evidence Kirron Kher ever said rape is part of Indian culture that cannot be stopped. Her actual recorded statements on rape condemned it and called for capital punishment, directly contradicting the fabricated quote circulating on Facebook/Twitter.

claim: We do not know where Covid-19 places among causes of death because the data is not published.
justification: Official cause-of-death data was being published well before October 2020 by agencies like the CDC and UK's PHE/ONS, and this data was already being used by researchers to estimate and debate where COVID-19 ranked among causes of death. The claim that such a ranking was unknowable due to lack of published data misrepresents the actual availability of mortality data at the time, though legitimate debates existed about classification accuracy and undercounting.

claim: Fly swatters are now available on Joe Biden's online store.
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (CBS News, CNN, The Hill, Newsweek) confirm that the Biden campaign began selling 'Truth Over Flies' fly swatters for $10 on its official online store within hours of the October 7, 2020 VP debate, and nearly 35,000 units sold out by the morning of October 8 — the exact date the claim was made.

claim: A campaign ad video for John Cornyn says that his plan would guarantee insurers must sell plans to any patient with preexisting conditions and will be covered in his plan.
justification: Cornyn's ad did make this claim, and the Washington Post Fact Checker specifically examined it, rating it 'misleading' because experts said his actual legislative proposal (the PROTECT Act) lacks explicit 'guaranteed issue' language and doesn't limit premiums, meaning insurers could still charge prohibitively high rates to sick patients, undermining the ad's implication of ACA-equivalent protection.

claim: The CDC has said over 98,000 people had non-COVID related deaths because of hospitals that were closed down for non-essential services
justification: The raw figure (~98,000-100,000 non-COVID excess deaths) does roughly match CDC excess-death data from that period, but the CDC never attributed those deaths specifically to hospitals being closed for non-essential services. A contemporaneous fact-check found the causal claim unconfirmed by CDC or other research, noting emergency rooms never closed and other explanations (e.g., fear of seeking care) were equally plausible.

claim: New Zealand spends less on pensions than most wealthy countries, spending 4.4 per cent of GDP
justification: Multiple independent sources (OECD data, academic papers, retirement commission analyses) consistently confirm New Zealand's pension spending as a share of GDP is well below the OECD average (historically ~8-9% OECD average vs NZ figures in the 4-5.5% range across different years and measures). The specific 4.4% figure cited for October 2020 falls within the documented range for net NZ Super spending trends, though exact figures vary slightly depending on whether gross or net (after-tax) spending is measured.

claim: Nigeria’s Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala has been appointed the new and first female Director-General of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
justification: Multiple sources confirm Okonjo-Iweala was not appointed WTO Director-General until 15 February 2021, taking office 1 March 2021. On the claim's publication date of 8 October 2020, she was only one of two finalist candidates and the selection process was in fact stalled due to U.S. opposition, with Yoo Myung-hee not withdrawing until February 2021. The claim's central assertion that she 'has been appointed' as of October 2020 is factually incorrect by about four months.

claim: When Joe Biden was US vice-president they took a month to act on information that might have saved Kayla Mueller, a humanitarian worker held hostage and sexually abused by the Islamic State terrorist group
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (Washington Post, CBS News) found that Obama approved the rescue plan almost immediately upon being presented with it in the Situation Room—one senior official called it 'the fastest presentation to decision' he'd seen—contradicting the claim that Obama/Biden 'hesitated for a month' after being informed. Any delay occurred earlier in the bureaucratic/intelligence-gathering process before the plan reached the White House, not from presidential inaction, and White House officials said they were 'mystified' by the one-month narrative.

claim: They [the Democrats] want to ... ban fracking.
justification: Independent fact-checks (AP, CNN, NBC) from the time of the debate concluded Pence's claim was false as applied to the Biden-Harris ticket's actual plan. Biden's written platform only called for banning new oil/gas permitting on public lands, not a nationwide fracking ban, and Biden and Harris repeatedly and explicitly denied any intent to ban fracking during the campaign. While Harris had personally supported a fracking ban during her own 2020 primary run, that was not the ticket's position once she became VP nominee, so attributing a fracking-ban agenda to 'them' (the Biden-Harris ticket) was judged false by multiple fact-checkers.

claim: Zimbabwe gets more than half of the African Export Import Bank loans.
justification: Zimbabwean fact-checking organization ZimFact investigated this exact claim by Biti and found it to be false, noting that Afreximbank's loans to the whole Southern Africa region (not just Zimbabwe) amounted to only 18% of its total loan portfolio, making it impossible for Zimbabwe alone to account for 'more than half' the bank's loans or balance sheet.

claim: US President Donald Trump following his positive diagnosis of COVID-19, was given treatment developed from the use of fetal tissue, made by the company Regeneron.
justification: Multiple independent outlets (CBS News, ABC News, Washington Post, MIT Technology Review, Newsweek) confirmed via Regeneron's own spokesperson that the antibody cocktail given to Trump was tested using the HEK293T cell line, which originated from a fetus aborted in the Netherlands in the 1970s. While the final injected product itself did not contain fetal tissue, the claim that the treatment's development/testing involved fetal-tissue-derived cells is accurate and corroborated by the manufacturer itself.

claim: U.S. mortalities this year are not materially different from the previous 5 years
justification: CDC final 2020 mortality data show the age-adjusted death rate rose 16.8% over 2019 (the largest single-year increase on record), with 528,891 more deaths than 2019 and a 1.8-year drop in life expectancy, the largest since WWII. Independent academic excess-mortality analysis (JAMA) also found a roughly 20% increase in deaths from March-August 2020 versus prior years. Contemporaneous fact-checks of similar social media claims about 2020 mortality being comparable to earlier years found them to be based on flawed data and math.

claim: The Democratic party has spent the last three and a half years trying to overturn the results of the last US election.
justification: Pence did make this statement verbatim at the Oct. 7, 2020 VP debate, but the underlying assertion conflates legitimate oversight actions (the Mueller Russia investigation and the 2019 impeachment over Ukraine) with an attempt to 'overturn' the 2016 election. Fact-checkers found no evidence of a party-wide effort to reverse the 2016 result, and Trump served his full term throughout the period in question, so the dramatic framing creates a false impression despite the real underlying events (investigation, impeachment) being accurately referenced.

claim: During the Obama/Biden administration, 18,000 people got clemency.
justification: Department of Justice data confirms Obama granted only 1,927 total clemency actions (1,715 commutations + 212 pardons), not 18,000 — nearly a tenfold overstatement. The 18,000 figure actually corresponds to the number of clemency petitions *denied*, not granted, during the Obama administration. PolitiFact rated this exact claim 'False,' and the Biden campaign itself acknowledged he misspoke and meant to say roughly 1,800.

claim: People in the UK who are required to self-isolate due to having tested positive for the COVID-19 virus will receive a support payment of £500 per week
justification: Boris Johnson did say '£500... per week' in this remark, but this was a misstatement of the actual policy. Official government guidance confirms the Test and Trace Support Payment was a one-off, lump-sum payment of £500 covering the entire self-isolation period (typically 10-14 days), not a weekly payment. Contemporary reporting explicitly noted Johnson's statement was incorrect.

claim: The PLAAF has shot down an Indian Sukhoi Su-30 fighter jet in Tibet.
justification: Multiple fact-checking outlets explicitly labeled this viral claim as fake, with headlines stating the IAF Su-30 was not shot down in Tibet. No official confirmation from India, China, or independent military sources exists for any such shootdown in October 2020, indicating the tweet spread disinformation.

claim: The wife of  Lal Bahadur Shastri (ex Prime minister of India) repaid his car loan after his death.
justification: Multiple independent sources, including a direct firsthand account from Shastri's son Anil Shastri as reported by Times of India, confirm that Shastri's widow Lalita Shastri repaid his ₹5,000 PNB car loan from her pension after declining the bank's offer to waive it following his death in 1966. The story is consistent across numerous reputable outlets over several years and the physical car is preserved at his memorial as corroborating evidence.

claim: Two E-6B Mercury planes were deployed because of US President Trump's positive COVID-19 test.
justification: U.S. Strategic Command and the Pentagon explicitly stated the E-6B flights were 'pre-planned missions' and that any timing relative to Trump's COVID announcement was 'purely coincidental.' Subsequent reporting confirmed these aircraft fly near-daily and were tracked on at least 20 days in the preceding month, undermining the idea they were specially deployed in response to the positive test.

claim: Other Countries Have Proved that the U.S. FDA Was Wrong to Withdraw Approval Of Hydroxychloroquine as COVID Drug
justification: The FDA's 2020 revocation was based on large randomized controlled trial data (notably the UK's RECOVERY trial) showing no mortality or recovery benefit from HCQ, and this finding was independently corroborated by the WHO's own international Solidarity trial, which also halted its HCQ arm for lack of benefit. Subsequent multi-country RCTs (e.g., the 11-country COPCOV trial) have continued to confirm HCQ's ineffectiveness against COVID-19, meaning the international scientific evidence base supports the FDA's decision rather than proving it wrong; countries that continued recommending HCQ did so despite, not because of, superior evidence.

claim: U.S. President Donald Trump and his wife, First Lady Melania Trump, have tested positive for COVID-19
justification: Multiple independent, high-quality sources (CBS News, NBC News, The Hill, KSAT) confirm that Trump tweeted he and Melania Trump had tested positive for COVID-19, a diagnosis also confirmed by the White House physician in an official statement. The tweet was sent just before 1 a.m. on October 2, 2020 Eastern time, meaning it was composed late on October 1, consistent with the claim's date.

claim: For a cumulative 29 of our 60 years of existence as a nation, we have been under military rule.
justification: This is a verified direct quote from Buhari's official Nigeria@60 Independence Day speech on 1 October 2020, confirmed by the State House transcript and multiple news outlets. The underlying arithmetic is also accurate: Nigeria was under military rule from 1966-1979 and 1983-1999, totaling approximately 29 years, a figure corroborated by multiple academic and historical sources discussing Nigeria's post-independence political history.

claim: Nigeria’s urban population at independence was approximately 7 million.
justification: World Bank historical data independently confirms Nigeria's 1960 urban population was approximately 6.9-7 million (6,942,788-6,955,737 depending on source), matching Buhari's stated figure almost exactly. A dedicated fact-check of this specific speech also confirmed the population claims were correct.

claim: Nigeria’s urban population at independence was approximately 7 million.
justification: Buhari's actual speech text states Nigeria's urban population at independence was 'approximately 7million,' and this matches World Bank historical data showing Nigeria's 1960 urban population at 6,942,788 — essentially identical to 7 million. An independent fact-check of this specific speech also confirmed his population claims as correct.

claim: At independence, Nigeria had a population of 45 million.
justification: Buhari's 2020 Independence Day speech explicitly stated Nigeria's population at independence was 45 million, and this is corroborated by multiple independent demographic sources including population pyramid data showing 45,053,782 people in 1960, and other historical analyses citing approximately 45 million or 45.1 million.

claim: It makes no sense for oil to be cheaper in Nigeria than in Saudi Arabia.
justification: Numerous independent Nigerian news outlets (TheCable, BusinessDay, Nairametrics, Guardian, Ripples Nigeria, The Gazette, etc.) all confirm Buhari made this exact statement word-for-word during his October 1, 2020 Independence Day broadcast, citing Nigeria's N161/litre price versus Saudi Arabia's N168/litre. The underlying price figures he cited were accurately reported. While critics argued the comparison omitted important context like minimum wage disparities, that is a critique of the argument's persuasiveness, not evidence that Buhari did not make this statement or that the cited prices were false.

claim: Nigeria has seen a 60% drop in government revenue
justification: Buhari did make this claim verbatim in his Oct 1, 2020 speech, and similar figures were repeated by Vice President Osinbajo. However, an independent fact-check found the claim's timeframe and basis unclear, and actual federal budget revenue data for 2020 (oil and non-oil) did not clearly support a 60% drop relative to any stated baseline, making the figure's accuracy unconfirmed by primary fiscal data.

claim: At independence, Nigeria had a population of 45 million.
justification: Buhari's October 1, 2020 speech stated Nigeria's population at independence was 45 million, and this was independently fact-checked and confirmed correct using UN and World Bank data showing 45.1 million in 1960. Multiple other independent sources corroborate this figure, including population pyramid data showing approximately 45,053,782.

claim: For a cumulative 29 of Nigeria's 60 years of existence as a nation, they have been under military rule
justification: Multiple independent academic sources confirm that Nigeria was under military rule for approximately 29 years between 1960 and 1999 (13 years from 1966-1979 plus 16 years from 1983-1999), and since Nigeria returned to uninterrupted civilian democratic rule in 1999 and remained so through 2020, the cumulative 29-year figure out of 60 years of independence cited by Buhari is accurate.

claim: 52% of Nigeria’s current population lives in urban areas
justification: Buhari's claim is directly supported by UN Population Division and World Bank data, which both estimated Nigeria's urban population at approximately 51.96% in 2020 — matching his stated 52% figure almost exactly. Independent fact-checking (Africa Check) confirmed this calculation using official UN/World Bank datasets.

claim: 52% of Nigeria’s current population lives in urban areas.
justification: Multiple independent sources (UN Population Division data, World Bank/IndexMundi figures, and a dedicated fact-check of this exact speech) confirm that Nigeria's urban population share in 2020 was approximately 51.96-52%, matching Buhari's statement almost exactly. A fact-check by The Insight explicitly verified this claim from the same speech as accurate.

claim: At independence in 1960  Nigeria had a population of 45 million.
justification: Buhari's 2020 speech stated Nigeria's population at independence in 1960 was 45 million, and this figure is confirmed by both UN/World Bank demographic estimates (45.1 million) and was explicitly verified as correct by independent fact-checkers at Africa Check who consulted demography experts.

claim: Judith Collins, the National Party leader stated that New Zealand was using more coal to generate electricity because of the oil and gas exploration ban.
justification: While Collins did repeatedly make this argument (including reportedly needling Ardern over coal use during the debate), New Zealand's then-Energy Minister and independent energy analysts both disputed the causal link, noting that exploration permits take years to reach production so the 2018 ban could not have caused coal increases observed by 2020, and that the actual drivers were low hydro lake levels and gas-field maintenance issues (e.g., at Pohokura), not the exploration ban.

claim: Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden received the questions for the first presidential debate in advance.
justification: The claim originated from conspiracy theorist Jerome Corsi's radio assertion that Chris Wallace gave Biden the debate questions in advance. A Fox News spokesperson directly refuted this to FactCheck.org, stating Wallace had not sent out any questions prior to the debate. No credible evidence or reporting has ever substantiated the claim, which was an unverified rumor circulating on debate day.

claim: Eating millets will protect you from Coronavirus.
justification: This specific claim was fact-checked by The Quint, which traced it to a viral Facebook message claiming millet-eaters don't get coronavirus. Medical experts, including a diabetes specialist and a scientist from the Indian Institute of Millets Research, explicitly stated there is no link between millets and coronavirus prevention, and the fact-check rated the claim 'False.' While millets have general nutritional/immunity benefits, the specific claim that eating them protects against or prevents COVID-19 is not supported by evidence.

claim: Claims that there were links between Trumps 2016 election campaign and Russia were part of a hoax that Hilary Clinton was behind.
justification: The claim echoes the 'Clinton plan intelligence' theory that surfaced on exactly September 29, 2020, but this theory is widely documented as an unproven conspiracy theory based on material that Durham's own investigation and multiple news outlets concluded was likely fabricated by Russian intelligence, not Clinton. Mueller's investigation separately documented real, extensive contacts between the Trump campaign and Russia, undermining the 'hoax' framing, and Durham was unable to substantiate that Clinton orchestrated any such plan.

claim: Sadiq Khan faked getting the flu jab as the plastic cap was still on the needle.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks confirm the photo was taken moments before Khan's actual flu injection, which explains the capped needle; the Mayor's office and corroborating photographic evidence (pharmacist preparing the injection site) confirm he genuinely received the flu vaccine on September 28, 2020. The 'faked' narrative misinterprets a pre-injection photo as evidence of deception.

claim: The Nigerian government is donating $600 million to Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden’s campaign.
justification: No credible news source, FEC record, or official statement supports the claim that Nigeria's government donated $600 million to Biden's 2020 campaign. US campaign finance law bans foreign national contributions entirely and caps all contributions at a tiny fraction of that sum, making the claim legally and practically impossible. This mirrors a nearly identical, already-debunked 2016 hoax claiming Nigeria's government gave $500 million to the Clinton campaign, indicating a recurring disinformation narrative rather than a real event.

claim: Olive Garden prohibits its employees from wearing face masks depicting the American flag.
justification: No primary source, news report, or official Olive Garden statement supports the specific claim that employees were barred from wearing American-flag-patterned face masks in 2020. Searches surfaced only an unrelated 2011 controversy over customers bringing physical flags into the restaurant (which Olive Garden explicitly denied having a policy against) and standard 2020 mask-wearing requirements with no mention of design restrictions.

claim: Distance between Gandhi and Green thread can determine if Rs 500 note is genuine or fake
justification: PIB and RBI have repeatedly and explicitly stated that the distance/proximity between Gandhi's portrait and the green security thread is NOT an indicator of whether a Rs 500 note is genuine or fake; both variants are valid legal tender, with the difference attributed to a minor printing variation, not counterfeiting.

claim: Donald Trump has not appoointed any black federal judges.
justification: Multiple contemporaneous fact-checks (AllSides, WUSA9) directly debunked this exact viral claim, confirming that at least eight Black federal judges had been nominated by Trump and confirmed by the Senate by September 2020, including judges like Terry Moorer, Rodney Smith, Rossie Alston, and Roderick Young. While Trump's appellate court appointments notably excluded any Black judges, the broad claim of zero Black federal judges overall is false.

claim: House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said of US employers, “Employers cutting hours is a good thing. It then gives that person time to pursue their dreams and passions.”
justification: PolitiFact explicitly fact-checked this exact quote and labeled it fake news, confirming Pelosi never said it. The phrase appears to originate from a fabricated meme image with no basis in any actual Pelosi speech, interview, or official transcript.

claim: The State of Massachusetts committed voter fraud by deleting over one million ballot images during the 2020 Presidential Election.
justification: Ayyadurai's claim that Massachusetts committed voter fraud by deleting over a million ballot images was fact-checked as false by the AP and Reuters, disputed by legal scholars, and denied by state officials who noted ballots are paper-based and that ballot-image capture was never enabled on certified machines (not 'deleted' after the fact). The 'over one million' figure is also internally implausible since only about 256,000 Republican primary votes were cast, and the claim conflates a September primary dispute with the November presidential election.

claim: George Soros connected to U-Haul operated by antifa activists distributed “shields, weapons & black bloc” to protesters in Louisville, Ky.
justification: The core event—a U-Haul distributing shields, riot gear and supplies to protesters in Louisville after the Breonna Taylor grand jury decision—is well documented on video. However, the 'George Soros connected' framing rests only on indirect links (two Bail Project board members being past 'Soros Justice Fellows'), and both the Open Society Foundations spokesperson and the Bail Project's national spokesperson explicitly denied any Soros funding of the truck or the renter's actions, with Lead Stories' fact-check concluding the Soros funding claim was not true.

claim: New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio officially ordered all police and citizens to stop sharing the booking photo of his daughter caught up during rioting
justification: Contemporaneous reporting shows de Blasio publicly criticized the police union (SBA) for leaking his daughter's arrest record and personal details, calling it 'unconscionable,' but there is no record of him issuing an 'official order' binding all police and citizens to stop sharing the photo. The tweet in question was removed because it violated Twitter's own private-information policy, not because of a mayoral directive. This claim appears to originate from a satire/fake-news site that mischaracterized the mayor's criticism as a formal order.

claim: False positives and rapid tests put the rate of infection near zero and that there will be no second wave of infections
justification: The claim that true infection rates were 'near zero' (attributing positive tests to false positives) and that no second wave would occur is directly contradicted by subsequent events: US COVID-19 cases, hospitalizations, and test positivity rates all surged to unprecedented record highs starting in October-November 2020, with daily cases rising from ~34,000 in September to over 150,000 by mid-November, and hospitalizations hitting all-time highs, confirmed by rising test positivity rates rather than mere testing artifacts.

claim: Former US vice-president Joe Biden is showing pretty severe signs of dementia.
justification: Contemporaneous fact-checks from the 2020 campaign period explicitly rejected claims that Biden showed signs of dementia, with a University of Michigan medicine professor telling Politifact that occasional word-finding difficulty 'does not mean he is senile or even that he has mild cognitive impairment.' A 2021 physician's report also described Biden as healthy and vigorous. While later years (2023-2025) brought more documented concerns about cognitive decline, the specific claim of 'pretty severe' dementia signs as of September 2020 was unsubstantiated and was characterized by independent fact-checkers as an unproven partisan attack.

claim: California Governor Gavin Newsom made it so that convicted sexual predators have lighter sentences.
justification: Multiple sources across the political spectrum confirm SB 145 did not change sentencing or criminal penalties for sex offenses at all — it only altered whether sex-offender registry placement was automatic or left to judicial discretion for consensual oral/anal sex offenses involving minors close in age, bringing it in line with existing discretion already given for vaginal intercourse cases. Even outlets critical of Newsom and the bill acknowledged that underlying criminal liability and punishment remained unchanged.

claim: U.S. Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg is the first woman in American history to lie in state at the U.S. Capitol.
justification: Numerous independent sources (NPR, The Hill, House.gov, UPI) confirm Ginsburg was formally designated as the first woman to 'lie in state' at the U.S. Capitol. The distinction from Rosa Parks (2005) is well-documented: Parks, a private citizen, 'lay in honor,' a related but technically different designation reserved for non-government officials, while 'lying in state' is reserved for government officials and military personnel.

claim: Black Lives Matter wants to destroy the nuclear family.
justification: BLM's official 'What We Believe' page did state it would 'disrupt the Western-prescribed nuclear family structure requirement,' and this language was removed right around September 21, 2020, matching the timing of Kirk's claim. However, the actual text framed this as supporting extended families/'villages' and included language affirming family-friendly spaces and parental participation, which critics note is different from literally wanting to 'destroy' families, making 'destroy' an exaggerated characterization of 'disrupt.'

claim: Basketball superstar Michael Jordan is joining NASCAR as a team owner.
justification: Multiple independent and primary sources (NASCAR.com, ESPN, AP via Bangor Daily News, law firm press release) confirm that on September 21, 2020, Michael Jordan and Denny Hamlin announced the formation of a NASCAR Cup Series team with Jordan as majority owner, officially entering NASCAR as a team owner starting in the 2021 season.

claim: Ruth Bader Ginsburg waged an "active campaign" to repeal the Mann Act and to lower the age of consent for sex
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (AP, Media Matters, PolitiFact-style outlets) found Ginsburg never waged a campaign to repeal the Mann Act or lower the age of consent; she made academic, gender-neutral-language critiques of statutory rape and Mann Act provisions in a 1974/1977 legal report, without ever stating a personal advocacy position on the age of consent, and the Mann Act was never repealed. The claim distorts a narrow academic argument into an 'active campaign,' which is not supported by the record.

claim: The Trump campaign only asked that Biden to release his list of potential Supreme Court nominees after Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg passed away.
justification: Multiple independent sources, including CNN's fact-check and the Trump campaign's own September 9, 2020 press release, confirm the Trump campaign and Trump himself repeatedly demanded Biden release a Supreme Court nominee list weeks before Ginsburg's September 18 death, including statements on September 9 and September 17, plus earlier demands in August and June. Biden's claim that the demand only arose after Ginsburg died is directly contradicted by this documented timeline.

claim: A man died in police custody after a 19th September 2020 anti-lockdown protest in London.
justification: Contemporaneous, detailed news coverage of the actual 19 September 2020 Trafalgar Square anti-lockdown/anti-vaccine protest (32 arrests, clashes with police, cleared by 6pm) makes no mention of any death in police custody. A death in custody following a high-profile London protest would have been major news and subject to an IOPC investigation, yet no such reporting exists in search results or Wikipedia's timeline of UK COVID-19 protests.

claim: Zimbabwe recorded its first coronavirus Infection before 20 February 2020.
justification: Multiple independent sources — Zimbabwe's Ministry of Health, VOA, Anadolu Agency, and peer-reviewed studies — consistently confirm that Zimbabwe's first COVID-19 case was recorded on 20 March 2020, a full month after the claimed date of 'before 20 February 2020'. The index patient was a 38-year-old Victoria Falls resident who returned from the UK on 15 March 2020, making an infection confirmed before 20 February 2020 impossible given the travel history described in official reports.

claim: Sightway Capital is owned by Two Sigma Investments.
justification: Extensive, consistent evidence from Two Sigma's own official website, PitchBook's corporate structure data, SEC filings, Crunchbase, and multiple news releases all confirm that Sightway Capital is Two Sigma's private equity subsidiary/business unit. Two Sigma Management, LLC serves as general partner of the advisory entity (TSPI, LP) that operates Sightway, establishing clear ownership/control.

claim: Donald Trump is in federal court trying to do away with the Affordable Care Act, 100 million people with preexisting conditions like your mom would not have to pay more for their insurance under now.”
justification: The Trump administration was indeed actively supporting a federal lawsuit (Texas v. US / California v. Texas) seeking to strike down the entire ACA, including its preexisting-condition protections, which was pending before the Supreme Court in fall 2020. The '100 million' figure, while on the high end, matches a widely-cited Avalere estimate (102 million) of Americans who could face higher premiums or coverage limitations without ACA protections, making it a defensible though not universally agreed-upon number—other estimates (like KFF's ~54 million for outright denial) are lower.

claim: Carlos Gimenez approved a 67% pay raise for himself and increased his own pension.
justification: The 67% salary increase from $150,000 to $250,000 in 2018 is well-documented and accurate, but it occurred through the standard county budget process approved by commissioners (after Gimenez requested a 'restoration' of salary), not as a unilateral act, and omits that he had earlier cut the mayoral salary by half upon taking office. The 'increased his own pension' portion is unsubstantiated by any source found; his documented pension is a separate pre-existing fire-chief pension unrelated to the mayoral salary change.

claim: Ventura County election officials are reducing voting locations in order to limit in-person voter turnout.
justification: It is true that Ventura County reduced in-person polling locations in 2020 (from roughly 400 to about 50), but this was part of the state-mandated Voter's Choice Act model, which paired fewer physical sites with universal mail ballots, expanded early voting days, and any-location voting — reforms explicitly designed to expand, not limit, voter access. No evidence supports the claim's core assertion that officials did this to suppress in-person turnout.

claim: Development Control Department of the Abuja Metropolitan Management Council (AMMC), an agency of the Federal Capital Territory Administration (FCTA)of Nigeria, in 2020 marked 37 Estates for demolition.
justification: Multiple independent news reports, including one published exactly on the claim's date (16 September 2020) by TheNigeriaLawyer, confirm that the AMMC's Development Control Department, under the FCTA, published a list of 37 named estates marked for demolition along the Abuja airport road for the centenary village project. The headline and full itemized list of 37 estates corroborate the figure precisely.

claim: A US voter can vote 4 times because he got 4 vote by mail forms.
justification: The specific Facebook post by James Snapp could not be located directly, but the claim matches a widely circulated and debunked 2020 narrative. Fact-checkers (AP, PolitiFact) and election security experts confirmed that receiving multiple mail ballot forms does not allow a person to vote multiple times, since signature verification and ballot logging systems prevent double voting, and such an attempt would constitute felony voter fraud.

claim: A Democratic Vice Presidential nominee, Kamala Harris, said that there will be "a federal tax on your home for slavery reparations."
justification: USA Today directly fact-checked this exact Facebook post and found no evidence Harris ever said or proposed a federal tax on homes for reparations. Harris's actual public statements on reparations focused on studying the issue and proposals like mental health funding or the LIFT Act tax credit, not a federal property tax. Additionally, such a tax would be constitutionally barred at the federal level, making the claim both factually unsupported and legally implausible.

claim: Fact Check: AARP Did NOT Spend 'Millions In TV Ads Targeting Republican Candidates' -- Nonprofit AARP Is Prohibited From Involvement In Any Political Campaigns
justification: AARP's nonpartisan status and legal prohibition on political campaign involvement as a 501(c)(4) organization is well-documented by AARP itself and confirmed by numerous independent fact-checkers (PolitiFact, Reuters, Lead Stories) across multiple similar claims in 2020. This specific Lead Stories fact-check fits a consistent pattern of debunked claims about AARP engaging in partisan political activity.

claim: McDonald’s take down American flags at their fast-food restaurants in support of Black Lives Matter and antifa (an umbrella term for far-left anti-fascism groups).
justification: Multiple independent fact-checkers (PolitiFact, Snopes, AP, Reuters) investigated this exact tweet from @Ron4Trump38 and found no evidence of any nationwide removal of American flags at McDonald's restaurants. McDonald's directly denied the rumor, stating the claims were not true, and fact-checkers noted the premise itself was illogical since neither BLM nor antifa are anti-American-flag movements.

claim: The rate of abortions under Democratic presidential administrations has actually fallen more precipitously.
justification: CDC and Guttmacher data do show steeper abortion rate declines during the Clinton and Obama administrations compared to Republican administrations since the 1980s, which supports the literal claim. However, this omits that the Democratic Carter administration saw a sharp increase, that CDC data changes (California dropping out) exaggerate the Clinton-era drop, and that fact-checkers like Snopes and PolitiFact conclude there is little evidence of a real correlation between presidential party and abortion rates once causation and state-level policy are considered.

claim: Iran has stockpiled 10 times as much enriched uranium as it had in 2016.
justification: IAEA's September 2020 quarterly report found Iran's low-enriched uranium stockpile had reached roughly 2,105 kg, about ten times the 300 kg limit imposed by the JCPOA—a limit that reflected the drastically reduced stockpile Iran held after Implementation Day in January 2016. Multiple independent sources (IAEA, ISIS nuclear analysis, Wikipedia's timeline) corroborate this 'tenfold' figure for the exact period Biden made the claim.

claim: unemployment rate in the state of Edo, Nigeria reduced from 25% to 19% during Godwin Obaseki's tenure.
justification: Multiple independent sources, including a dedicated fact-check, confirm that NBS data showed Edo's unemployment rate falling from 25.1% to 19% during the relevant period, and the fact-check explicitly stated the underlying data was correct (only the infographic's design/attribution to NBS was misleading). There is minor inconsistency across sources on whether the 19% figure was for Q2 2019 or Q2 2020, but the core 25.1%-to-19% claim is consistently corroborated.

claim: Netflix tweets that its content is "mostly pedophilia-free" in response to criticism over its streaming of "Cuties"
justification: The quote originates from the Babylon Bee, a well-known satire website, not from an actual Netflix tweet or statement. There is no evidence Netflix made this statement; it was a satirical fabrication in response to the 'Cuties' controversy.

claim: These unlicensed vaccines will be administered by non-medical staff, such as your employer in the UK.
justification: The claim distorts actual 2020 UK regulatory changes (expanding the trained vaccinator workforce and allowing temporary emergency authorisation of vaccines under strict MHRA safeguards) into a false narrative that untrained employers would inject staff with unapproved vaccines. Elnaugh has a well-documented history of spreading anti-vaccine misinformation during this period, including calling for Chris Whitty to 'hang' over vaccine policy for children, consistent with promoting distorted claims about vaccine regulations.

claim: Joe Biden’s own chief of staff said that when Biden managed swine flu in 2009, they quote, “Did every possible thing wrong.”
justification: Ron Klain did say 'we did every possible thing wrong' about H1N1 in a 2019 speech, so the quote itself is accurate. But Trump's framing — that this was Biden personally 'managing' swine flu and doing everything wrong — omits that Klain wasn't involved in the H1N1 response and was speaking about the administration generally, that Klain later clarified the remark referred specifically to vaccine-production difficulties, and that independent assessments rated the actual 2009 response as largely effective.

claim: Antifa Admit to Igniting Fires All Over The Country To Draw Attention To Climate Change
justification: The claim is based on a screenshot from a fake 'Scarsdale Antifa' Twitter account that had already been identified as a known impersonator account since 2017. Multiple law enforcement agencies (FBI Portland, Oregon State Police, local sheriffs) and independent fact-checkers (PolitiFact, FactCheck.org, USA Today, Lead Stories) investigated and found no evidence of antifa involvement in starting any of the 2020 West Coast wildfires, explicitly debunking this specific claim.

claim: CDC announces that ordinary (non-N95) masks (which most people are wearing) will do nothing to protect you against wildfire smoke because they do not catch small particles
justification: Multiple independent sources, including the CDC's own Facebook post and contemporaneous news reporting from the Washington Examiner, Fox21, Fast Company, and KQED, confirm that the CDC stated in September 2020 that cloth masks (non-N95) offer little to no protection against wildfire smoke because they do not catch the small particles found in smoke. The claim's phrasing closely matches a widely-reported tweet by Alex Berenson quoting the CDC's actual statement.

claim: The upper age-limit for Muslim candidates for the UPCS (i.e. Union Public Service Commission for recruitment to higher Civil Services of the Government of India) exam is relaxed to be higher than that of other applicants
justification: Official UPSC notifications base age relaxations solely on social/economic categories (SC, ST, OBC, disability, defense service), not religion; Muslims in general category get the same 32-year limit as Hindus, and only Muslims who qualify for OBC/SC/ST status get relaxations available to all members of those categories regardless of religion. India's Supreme Court explicitly found this claim, made by Sudarshan News's Suresh Chavhanke, to be a 'factually incorrect statement' and part of an insidious attempt to vilify Muslims, and the I&B Ministry separately deemed it misleading.

claim: Greater number of Muslim aspirants are suddenly taking the UPCS (i.e. Union Public Service Commission for recruitment to higher Civil Services of the Government of India) exam
justification: Independent fact-checks (Alt News/The Wire) examined the same data cited by Sudarshan News and found the 'sudden increase' claim was constructed by selectively omitting 2018 data, which actually showed a decrease; other reporting noted a steep decline in Muslim candidates from at least one targeted institution. The Supreme Court and the I&B Ministry also found the underlying 'infiltration' narrative baseless and in violation of broadcasting norms, with any genuine rise in Muslim UPSC aspirants attributed to legitimate outreach and awareness efforts rather than a sudden, suspicious spike.

claim: the Indian Government set up 5 coaching centres for UPSC exams, 4 of which were in Muslim universities.
justification: The specific numerical claim is accurate: The Print and other sources confirm the government set up five UPSC coaching centres between 2009-2010, four of which (Jamia Millia Islamia, Jamia Hamdard, Aligarh Muslim University, and Maulana Azad National Urdu University) are at Muslim-affiliated universities, with the fifth at Bhimrao Ambedkar University. However, important context is that these centres serve all underprivileged communities (SC/ST/women/minorities), not exclusively Muslims, which is the context Sudarshan News omitted when using this fact to allege favoritism.

claim: US Congress voted 49-46 to add the repeal of Section 230 — legislation which shields online platforms from liability for user-generated content — into the country’s annual defense bill in December 2020
justification: Multiple independent sources (TechCrunch, CNBC, Washington Post, CBS News, NetChoice, Wikipedia) confirm that Section 230 repeal was never added to the NDAA. The House passed the NDAA 355-78 and the Senate 84-13 without any Section 230 language; Trump vetoed the bill specifically because it lacked a Section 230 repeal, and Congress overrode the veto without ever adding such language. No '49-46' vote on a Section 230 repeal in the NDAA appears in any legislative record.

claim: 80 million ballots for the US November 3 2020 election will be mailed to US voters who didn’t request them.
justification: Trump did make this exact claim at the September 7, 2020 Labor Day press conference, confirmed by the official White House transcript. However, multiple independent fact-checks (PolitiFact, CNN, NBC) found the claim itself to be false: the actual number of truly unsolicited/automatically-mailed ballots was about 44 million (in nine states plus D.C.), roughly half of Trump's 80 million figure, which conflated the total expected mail-in ballots (including those actively requested by voters) with unsolicited ones.

claim: PGA star Bubba Watson wrote a post that says, "I see signs all over saying black lives matter. I’m just trying to figure out which black lives matter.”
justification: Multiple independent sources, including Golf News Net and Lead Stories' fact-check, confirm that Bubba Watson never wrote this viral Facebook post and publicly denied authorship on Twitter. The post was fabricated and falsely attributed to him, making the claim that this is something Watson actually said false, regardless of who (e.g., Fred Childs) may have shared it on Facebook.

claim: Wearing a face mask can cause pleurisy.
justification: Multiple independent medical experts (Duke, Yale, University of Alabama pulmonologists, American Lung Association's chief medical officer) and fact-checking organizations (AP, local news Trust Index investigations) unanimously found no medically plausible mechanism linking mask-wearing to pleurisy. Masks allow free gas exchange and the lungs have natural bacterial clearance mechanisms, and decades of healthcare workers wearing masks for long shifts show no pattern of pleurisy cases.

claim: Video of a man blowing vape smoke through various face masks shows that they do not help prevent the spread of coronavirus.
justification: Independent experts (Mayo Clinic, Johns Hopkins, University of Florida, UT Austin, Texas A&M) and multiple fact-checkers reviewed this viral video and concluded it does not prove masks are ineffective. They explained that vape smoke vastly overrepresents real respiratory droplet volume, that masks reduce the distance and forward travel of exhaled particles even if some escape at the edges, and that the video creates a false equivalency between gaseous vapor and virus-laden respiratory droplets.

claim: Tweet shows Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) president Raj Thackeray showing their support of Bollywood actress Kangana Ranaut.
justification: Multiple fact-checks (Newsmeter/BOOM) identified @RealThackeray/@ThackerayOffic as a fake, unverified impostor account created in July 2020 with ~11,000 followers, distinct from Raj Thackeray's real verified handle @RajThackeray (created 2017, ~750,000 followers), which had no tweets about Kangana Ranaut. Raj Thackeray himself did not air support for Kangana Ranaut; the real MNS activity at the time was a cinema-wing leader criticizing her, not supporting her.

claim: Willie Obiano, the Governor of Anambra State in Nigeria, procured over 100 SUVs as gifts for Anambra state traditional monarchs.
justification: Multiple independent sources, including the official Anambra State government website, confirm Governor Willie Obiano presented over 100 Innoson-made SUVs (reported variously as 126, 130, or 151) to Anambra traditional rulers/monarchs in early September 2020. The exact count varies by source depending on whether suspended monarchs were excluded, but all figures exceed 100, supporting the core claim.

claim: Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray has come forward in support of Bollywood actress Kangana Ranaut and would welcome her back to Mumbai, India.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (Aaj Tak, NewsMeter/Dailyhunt) identified this exact tweet as a viral fake, confirming no such tweet existed on Raj Thackeray's verified Twitter account. Contemporary reporting (TheIndianExpress/ThePrint) instead shows Thackeray issued gag orders silencing his party on the issue and, when he did speak, criticized Kangana for her remarks about Mumbai Police rather than welcoming her back to Mumbai.

claim: Over the past 40 years, the Uyghur population in Xinjiang, in China, grew from 5.55 million to 12 million.
justification: The tweet is authentic and the 5.55 million to ~12 million figures match other official Chinese government statements and census data from the same period (1978 figure of 5.55 million Uyghurs growing to 11.62-12.71 million by 2018-2020). The core numerical claim is supported by China's own official statistics, though independent analysts note this framing omits that Han population growth rates in Xinjiang have outpaced Uyghur growth rates in recent decades, and that Uyghur birth rates sharply declined after 2017.

claim: Raj Thackeray tweeted "On 9 September, Hindu lioness Kangana Ranaut will be given a grand welcome in Maharashtra’s capital, Mumbai."
justification: Fact-checkers found that a separate fake tweet attributed to Raj Thackeray about Kangana Ranaut's office demolition circulated in this exact period (Sept 2020) from an impersonator account, and confirmed his verified account posted no tweets about Kangana Ranaut at all. No primary source or credible news report was found confirming the specific 'Hindu lioness... grand welcome' quote, despite extensive media coverage of the Kangana-Shiv Sena controversy at the time.

claim: People are trying to lower the legal age of consent to four years old in the U.S.
justification: Fact-checkers examining this exact viral claim from August/September 2020 found it had no identifiable source, no named individuals or groups, and no supporting legislation anywhere in the U.S. The age of consent in all U.S. states ranges from 16 to 18, and there is no evidence of any effort to lower it to four years old; attempts to link it to California's SB 145 were also debunked since that law does not alter the age of consent.

claim: Sturgis Motorcycle Rally resulted in no more positive Covid results than the rest of the state, South Dakota, average stating 88 positive tests to Sturgis Rally, 0.02% infection rate of attendees.
justification: By September 3, 2020, state and CDC reporting already documented case counts far exceeding the claimed '88,' including 124+ in-state and 290+ multi-state cases, rising to 649 total cases in a later CDC study. South Dakota's own statewide positivity rate was climbing sharply during this period (6% to 9%), and Meade County (home to Sturgis) saw a massive spike directly tied to the rally, contradicting the claim that the rally caused no more infections than the state average.

claim: Viral message claims that all Haldiram’s food products were banned in USA
justification: Fact-checkers (NewsMeter) explicitly labeled the viral claim that USFDA banned all Haldiram snacks as FALSE, noting it recycled outdated 2015/2017 import-refusal news and a debunked marble-dust rumor, while Haldiram's products were being sold legally (via Amazon) in the US as of 2019-2020. India's food safety regulator chief also publicly rebutted the forward in May 2020.

claim: Voters in North Carolina can send their Mail-in vote and then go to the polling place to vote again to check that their mail-in vote has been counted.
justification: Multiple independent news sources (CNN, NBC, NPR, Fox News, ABC News, CBS News) confirm Trump told North Carolina voters on September 2, 2020 to mail in their ballot and then go to their polling place to check if it was counted, voting in person if it hadn't been tabulated.
