This is exactly what the claim describes, and it is well-documented via direct quotes from the WECT-TV interview and subsequent tweets.

claim: "Jihadists" attacked a Temple in West Bengal and charred the Hindu deity Kali
justification: Multiple independent sources — the temple's own secretary, Murshidabad Police, the Superintendent of Police, and West Bengal Police — all confirmed the Kali idol fire was accidental (caused by a devotional lamp), with no broken locks, no theft, and no communal angle. Arjun Singh's claim of a 'jihadist' attack was explicitly contradicted by both temple authorities and law enforcement who investigated the scene directly.

claim: U.S. citizens should show up at polling places on Election Day and cast an in-person ballot if poll workers can’t confirm that their mail-in ballot was received.
justification: Multiple independent sources (WECT's own report, CNN, NBC, NPR, Al Jazeera) confirm Trump told voters in his Sept. 2, 2020 WECT interview to mail in their ballot and then go to the polls, and if it hadn't been tabulated/counted, they could vote in person. This matches the claim's description almost verbatim. The surrounding context—that this was widely criticized as effectively encouraging illegal double voting—doesn't change the accuracy of the specific attributed statement.

claim: More cops have died from COVID this year than have been killed on patrol.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (PolitiFact, Washington Post) and two separate nonprofit tracking organizations (Officer Down Memorial Page and NLEOMF) confirmed that COVID-19 killed more law enforcement officers in 2020 than all other on-duty causes combined, including gunfire, car accidents, etc. Even when narrowing the definition to exclude corrections officers and other edge-case classifications, COVID-19 remained the single leading cause of officer deaths, and later academic research corroborated the finding.

claim: US President Trump issued an executive order for the White House to take over all electrical grids, which will include internet servers, broadcasting systems and electronic systems
justification: The real executive order Trump signed (May 1, 2020, EO 13920) only addressed foreign-made equipment in the bulk-power transmission system (lines rated 69kV+) and explicitly excluded local distribution facilities; it did not give the White House control over 'all electrical grids' and made no mention of internet servers or broadcasting systems. No reporting from mainstream outlets, the Department of Energy, or the White House itself supports the sweeping takeover described in the Facebook claim.

claim: US President Trump issued an executive order to reopen states in lockdown during COVID-19 pandemic; governors who refuse will be sued
justification: No executive order by Trump ordering states to reopen, with threats to sue non-compliant governors, has ever been documented. The closest real event was Trump's April 2020 tweets/statements claiming 'total authority' to reopen states, which fact-checkers (PolitiFact, NPR, CNBC, CBS) rated as false since that authority constitutionally belongs to governors, not the president. By September 2020, states were still independently managing their own reopening plans without any such federal order.

claim: Igbo people In Nigeria (Igbo people are found in southeastern Nigeria) are the richest people per capita in Africa.
justification: A dedicated fact-check (Daily Trust/Dubawa) found no official data exists on GDP or income by ethnicity in Nigeria, and the NBS spokesperson called the claim 'not statistically correct.' Available proxy data (state poverty rates) is mixed—some Igbo states do better than the national average, but the South-East region overall had higher poverty than the national rate, and several non-Igbo Nigerian states fared better. Nigeria as a whole also ranks far below several smaller African economies in GDP per capita, making the specific 'richest per capita in Africa' claim unsupportable by any verifiable metric, though Igbo entrepreneurial success and wealth are real and widely noted.

claim: The US military will check purity and distribute COVID-19 vaccines in US.
justification: Fact-checks from AP and Reason, published around the same time as this claim, found that Trump's repeated assertions that 'the military... is going to distribute the vaccine' were inaccurate; an HHS official stated no federal official would touch the vaccine before it was injected into Americans, and actual distribution was run through civilian/commercial channels (CDC, McKesson, FedEx/UPS) with the military playing only a supporting logistics/planning role.

claim: A 21 year old can have sex with an 11-year-old, and not be listed on the sex registry as a sex offender
justification: This claim misrepresents real legislation (like California's SB 145) that gave judges discretion only in close-in-age statutory rape cases, not in cases involving an adult and a child as young as 11. Legal sources confirm that sex offender registration exemptions ('Romeo and Juliet' provisions) require both a small age gap (typically 2-4 years) and an older minor victim (usually 13+), and that offenses against children under 13-14 (like what a 21-year-old having sex with an 11-year-old would constitute) trigger mandatory registration in virtually every US jurisdiction. No search result identified any actual law allowing the scenario described.

claim: In Belfast, the digital sector employs 26 per cent of the workforce.
justification: Multiple independent sources (Silicon Republic, GOV.UK press release, Lorien Global) corroborate that Tech Nation's analysis in 2020 found Belfast's digital tech sector employed approximately 26% of the city's workforce, consistent with the claim attributed to The Times on 1 September 2020.

claim: It's NOT a SECOND WAVE of COVID-19 coming soon. It's the NORMAL COLD / FLU SEASON
justification: The claim conflates COVID-19 with ordinary seasonal cold/flu illness, but COVID-19 is a distinct, more severe disease, and historical data show the 2020-2021 flu season was abnormally mild (not 'normal') due to COVID mitigation measures, while COVID-19 itself caused a massive, well-documented surge in cases and deaths that fall/winter that was tracked separately from flu surveillance.

claim: Face masks cause hypoxia.
justification: Multiple fact-checks, medical experts, and a controlled peer-reviewed study (50 subjects) found zero cases of hypoxemia from wearing cloth or surgical masks at rest or during exercise. Experts state there is no evidence masks impair oxygen delivery in healthy individuals, with any risk limited to severe pre-existing respiratory disease and even then typically remaining within normal physiologic range.

claim: US cable news channel Fox News is not available in Canada due to media legislation in the country.
justification: Fox News has been authorized for distribution on Canadian cable/satellite since 2004 and remains on the CRTC's approved list; fact-checkers in 2012, 2014, and 2021 specifically debunked the claim that media legislation bars it from Canada. The original 2003 rejection was about protecting Canadian broadcasters from foreign competition, not any truth-in-news law, and no such law has ever blocked Fox News from Canadian airwaves.

claim: 558 people were killed by the police in 2018, while 201 people died in police custody
justification: Africa Check's fact-check of this exact claim, based on IPID's 2017/18 annual data, rated it 'correct': 558 people died as a result of police action and IPID recorded 201 incidents of death in police custody for that period. The only minor caveat noted by fact-checkers is that the 201 figure counts 'incidents' rather than strictly individual deaths, but this does not materially undermine the claim.

claim: Jacob Blake raped a 14 year old teenage girl.
justification: Extensive contemporaneous reporting (Wikipedia, NBC News, CNN, Kenosha News, Fox News) shows Blake was charged with third-degree sexual assault involving the adult mother of his children, whom he had known for eight years, not a 14-year-old girl. There is no credible source corroborating that the victim was a minor; the claim misrepresents both the age of the accuser and the nature of the charge.

claim: Islamic study is a subject in UPSC exam
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (Logically Facts, DFRAC, Alt News, Latestly) examined the official UPSC syllabus for the Civil Services exam and all other UPSC-conducted exams and found no subject called 'Islamic Studies' among the compulsory papers, optional subjects, or language options. The claim traces to an August 2020 Sudarshan News promo that was publicly refuted by serving IPS/IAS officers and the IPS Officers' Association at the time, and it has been repeatedly debunked whenever it resurfaces on social media.

claim: Biden has promised to abolish the production of American oil, coal, shale, and natural gas.
justification: Multiple contemporaneous reports and fact-checks confirm Biden never promised to abolish U.S. oil, coal, shale, or natural gas production. His actual platform called for banning new oil/gas permits on federal lands and ending subsidies, while he repeatedly stated fracking would continue as a 'bridge' fuel and that he would not end the industry nationwide. Fact-checkers explicitly rated similar Trump/Pence claims about Biden 'ending fracking' as 'mostly false.'

claim: Duterte has signed order to open nuclear power plant.
justification: As of August 2020, Duterte had only signed EO 116 (July 24, 2020), which created an inter-agency committee to study the feasibility of nuclear energy and the mothballed Bataan plant — it did not order the plant to be opened. The actual policy EO (164) committing to nuclear energy wasn't signed until February 2022, and even that only directed further study/recommendations on reviving the plant, not an order to open it. The claim mischaracterizes a feasibility-study order as an order to open the plant.

claim: Donald Trump said "We have spent nearly $2.5 trillion on completely rebuilding our military, which was very badly depleted when I took office."
justification: Trump did say this exact line in his Aug 27, 2020 RNC speech, but independent fact-checks (Roll Call/FactCheck.org, Breaking Defense/CSIS experts) found the $2.5 trillion figure misleading: it represents total DoD budget outlays (actually ~$2.9 trillion inflation-adjusted for 2017-2020), not spending specifically on 'rebuilding' equipment, which made up only about 20% of that total and was actually lower as a share than under Obama. The claim that the military was 'completely rebuilt' with this spending and was previously 'very badly depleted' is not supported by the budget breakdown.

claim: The Edo State government of Nigeria receives 600 million naira monthly as a security vote.
justification: Ize-Iyamu did repeatedly make this exact claim during the 2020 campaign, as confirmed by multiple contemporaneous news reports quoting him directly. However, Nigerian 'security votes' are notoriously undisclosed and not itemized in public budgets, and the N600 million figure was explicitly presented as his campaign's own estimate/calculation rather than an official or independently verified figure; other sources from the same period cite different estimates (e.g., roughly $2 million monthly), making the precise monthly amount impossible to independently confirm.

claim: Donald Trump said "Last month, I took on Big Pharma. You think that is easy? I signed orders that would massively lower the cost of your prescription drugs."
justification: Trump did say this exact quote in his August 27, 2020 RNC acceptance speech, and he had indeed signed four executive orders on drug pricing in July 2020. However, PBS NewsHour's contemporaneous fact-check rated the claim itself as 'quite misleading' because the orders had not yet taken effect, one order's text wasn't even publicly available, and experts said the measures would be unlikely to produce significant drug price reductions for most Americans.

claim: This Democratic Party of Joe Biden is pushing the so-called Green New Deal. If given power, they would essentially ban animal agriculture and eliminate gas-powered cars.
justification: Ernst did make this statement verbatim at the 2020 RNC, but its central assertion—that Biden/Democrats would 'essentially ban animal agriculture and eliminate gas-powered cars'—is false. PolitiFact rated the claim False, noting Biden never endorsed the Green New Deal resolution, which itself does not call for ending animal agriculture or gas-powered cars, and a Stanford climate scientist called the causal link 'unfounded.' Multiple independent fact-checks (The Hill, PolitiFact, Daily Iowan) reached the same conclusion.

claim: Joe Biden is for open borders, sanctuary cities, free lawyers and health care for illegal immigrants.
justification: Contemporaneous fact-checks (NPR and others) of this exact RNC speech found that Biden did not support 'open borders,' did not promise 'free lawyers' (his plan added asylum officers/interpreters, not free legal counsel), and did not propose taxpayer-subsidized 'free health care' for illegal immigrants (only emergency care already mandated by law, or an unsubsidized public-option buy-in). Only the 'sanctuary cities' portion accurately reflects Biden's stated 2020 position of limiting local-federal immigration enforcement cooperation.

claim: The first night of the US Republican National Convention had 128.4 million viewers
justification: Nielsen's official data and multiple independent news outlets (Forbes, Deadline, NBC News, Reuters, Daily Beast) consistently reported first-night RNC 2020 TV viewership at approximately 15.8 to 17 million, not 128.4 million. No credible source, including combined TV-plus-streaming totals for either convention that year, comes close to 128.4 million for the RNC's opening night.
